content: 1. Studies comparing cases identified through active screening with those detected passively have consistently shown that individuals identified via screening are less likely to have smear-positive tuberculosis. This finding aligns with the observation that smear testing is often the primary diagnostic method in routine passive case detection, as seen in South Africa, where culture testing is typically reserved for those who test positive on initial screening. 2. A significant challenge in evaluating these studies is the lack of detailed information on the diagnostic procedures applied to passively detected cases. Unfortunately, such data were unavailable for most studies. 3. The proportion of smear-positive cases with a high smear grading (e.g., 3+) is likely a more accurate indicator of disease severity. In studies from Cambodia, India, and South Africa, the proportion of high smear grading was lower among screened cases compared to passively detected cases. 4. Radiographic findings in studies from various regions, including Ross (1977), Wang (2000), and LeBue (2004), consistently showed less extensive disease among screened cases. However, none of these studies confirmed all cases bacteriologically, raising the possibility of false positives among individuals with mild radiographic abnormalities. 5. Length-time bias cannot be excluded as a factor in these studies. For example, in an Indian study (Santha 2003), the proportion of patients reporting a delay of less than three months from symptom onset to diagnosis was twice as high among screened cases compared to passively detected cases. 6. A study in the United Kingdom among homeless individuals found that the average diagnostic delay was three times longer for passively detected cases compared to those identified through screening (Story 2012). 7. In a Brazilian community trial, there was little difference in reported diagnostic delays between intervention and control groups (Miller 2010). Similarly, a cross-sectional study in Ethiopia found that 54% of screened individuals experienced delays longer than 90 days, compared to 58% of unscreened individuals (Shargie 2006a). 8. A community-based randomized controlled trial in Ethiopia found that the proportion of participants with delays longer than 90 days was 22% lower in intervention communities compared to control communities (41% vs. 63%). 9. Recall bias and differences in symptom perception and interpretation may have influenced the findings of these studies, limiting the overall quality of evidence on self-reported delays. 10. A study from the former Czechoslovakia in the 1960s revealed that 79% of individuals with smear-positive TB developed the disease within 36 months of a previously normal chest X-ray. This suggested that a screening interval of 2–3 years was too long to significantly reduce diagnostic delays and disease severity at diagnosis. 11. A 2011 study among South African miners compared 6-monthly chest X-ray screening with 12-monthly screening. Cases detected in the 6-monthly arm had less extensive disease at diagnosis, as judged by radiology, and lower TB-specific mortality at two months. However, the mortality reduction at 12 months was not statistically significant. 12. Evidence of very low quality suggests that treatment outcomes among individuals identified through screening are similar to those identified through passive case detection. Six studies from Cambodia, India, Nepal, South Africa, and Zambia reported comparable treatment success rates for screened and passively detected cases. 13. Differences in baseline characteristics, such as disease severity and age, between screened and passively detected cases were not controlled for in these studies, making it difficult to interpret the lack of difference in treatment outcomes. 14. A cohort study among South African miners found that the adjusted relative risk of death was 82% lower for individuals identified through routine screening compared to those identified passively. However, length-time bias and residual confounding cannot be excluded. 15. Initial default rates (i.e., individuals diagnosed with TB who did not start treatment) were higher among screened cases compared to passively detected cases in studies from India. However, no deaths were reported among those who defaulted after being screened, whereas 19% of passively detected defaulters died. 16. Nine additional studies reported initial default rates among screened cases, ranging from 4% to 26%, with a weighted mean of 13%. For settings outside India, initial default rates among passively detected cases were not reported but may be high, with poor outcomes. 17. No studies reported morbidity outcomes beyond conventional TB treatment outcomes, such as relapse, acquired drug resistance, chronic sequelae, or quality-adjusted life years lost. 18. There is moderate-quality evidence that implementing low-sensitivity screening approaches does not affect TB epidemiology. However, more intensive screening may reduce the burden of TB in the screened population, though the evidence ranges from very low to low quality. 19. Five studies assessed the impact of TB screening on the burden of TB in the general population. Two randomized controlled trials (ZAMSTAR in Zambia/South Africa and a trial in Brazil) found mixed results, with some reductions in TB prevalence and incidence, though not all findings were statistically significant. 20. A community-based trial in Zimbabwe (DETECTB) found a 40% reduction in TB prevalence over three years in both intervention arms, though the study lacked a control group without screening. 21. Secular trends in screened populations were assessed in Cambodia and the United States. In Cambodia, TB notification rates were 62% lower in screened communities compared to national trends. In the United States, a program of mandatory screening and treatment in homeless shelters was associated with a nearly 90% reduction in TB notifications over 10 years. 22. Overall, the evidence for the impact of screening on TB epidemiology in the community remains weak. Most studies have significant methodological limitations and assess only a limited number of screening approaches in specific epidemiological contexts.
